newsitem.title: USA: Wholesale prices fall 0.1 percent in March.
newsitem.headline: Wholesale prices fall 0.1 percent in March.

text.p: Prices at the wholesale level fell for the third month in a row in March, the Labour Department said Friday, new evidence that fears of a major breakout of inflation may as yet be unfounded.
The department said the Producer Price Index fell 0.1 percent after dropping 0.4 percent in February and 0.3 percent percent in January.

However, the picture was less benign when the often-volatile food and energy sector was excluded. This so-called core rate, which economists believe more closely tracks inflation, rose 0.4 percent after falling 0.1 percent in February.
Wall Street had estimated that overall prices would be unchanged while the core rate would be up 0.1 percent.

Investors reacted to the rise in the core rate by pushing the 30-year U.S. Treasury bond down 20/32 of a point, or $6.25 on a $1,000 bond. Its yield, which moves in the opposite direction, rose to 7.16 percent from 7.11 percent Thursday.

"The PPI core rate was much higher than expected," said Melanie Hardy, an economist at Bear Stearns & Co. Inc. "But aircraft added 0.2 percent to the core rate and certainly aircraft doesn't appear in people's consumption basket, so I don't think that is indicative of any sort of pickup in industrial prices," she added.
But Astrid Adolfson, of MCM Moneywatch Inc., cautioned that the report showed "There might be some more inflation in the pipeline than what we had thought."
The department said energy prices, which fell 3.4 percent after dropping 1.2 percent in February, were the major ingredient in the decline in overall prices.
Gasoline prices tumbled 4.0 percent after retreating 3.1 percent in February, while home heating oil plummeted 9.9 percent after falling 1.1 percent in the prior month.
Food prices, however, rose 0.9 percent in the month after falling 0.3 percent in February. The department said the increase reflected a rise in beef, fish and vegetables prices.
Goods at the intermediate level of production that require additional processing fell 0.6 percent, while so-called crude goods at the early level of production fell 6.9 percent.
It was the first time wholesale prices fell three months in a row since consecutive declines in May through August 1993.
